newsitem.title: USA: Texas House to begin debate on tax cut plan.
newsitem.headline: Texas House to begin debate on tax cut plan.

text.p: The Texas House of Representatives Thursday was expected to begin debate on part two of a tax relief plan that would mean a $1 billion net reduction in the property taxes Texans pay.
Part one of the plan, House Joint Resolution Four, was passed by a 114-35 vote margin late Wednesday night, Janet Warren, press secretary to House Speaker Pete Laney, said.

HJR Four is a proposed constitutional amendment accompanying the tax cut bill, which is called House Bill Four. The joint resolution is needed to alter some aspects of the state's constitution to allow for HB Four, Warren said.
Monday, Laney postponed a scheduled Tuesday vote on the tax cut plan after some 235 proposed amendments to the package were pre-filed by Monday night's deadline.
Though exact figures were not immediately accessible, Warren said roughly 40 of those amendments pertained to the resolution that passed Wednesday night, while nearly 200 applied to House Bill Four.
"There are substantially more amendments proposed for the bill than there were for the HJR, so they will get as far as they can on that today," she said.
Warren declined to speculate on exactly when the House bill would be ready for a vote.
"You never know how many people are going to want to debate something, but I guess it would be fair to say that the bill could take as long as two days," Warren said.

According to a synopsis of HB4 distributed earlier, the proposal would cut residential rates on average by 50 percent with a cap of 70 cents per $100 for maintenance and operation. It caps business rates at $1.05 per $100. It would also pass property tax cuts onto renters.
The proposal also calls for the state to pay for 80 percent of public education costs, and would provide state matching funds to help districts retire bond debt and build new facilities.

The plan would pay for the property tax cuts with $1 billion from surplus state funds, and by eliminating a variety of exemptions. It would apply franchise tax to partnerships, but not sole proprietors. It would eliminate 30 sales tax exemptions, five motor fuels tax exemptions, and increase taxes on tobacco products and alcoholic beverages.
